extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, legal counsel for news organizations, and news-agency executives
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and operative criteria (from a 1917 U.S. district-court complaint and decision) for when a news service may prevent competitors from appropriating and selling its collected news prior to general publication, and what methods constitute unlawful/pirating conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality obligations under Associated Press by-laws
rubrics_metrics.description: News received through complainant's service is received exclusively for the purpose of publication in the specific newspaper, language and place specified in the member's certificate; members shall permit no other use; no member shall furnish or permit anyone in his employ to furnish any of complainant's news in advance of publication to any person who is not a member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (paraphrased from the bill and affidavits): the by-laws require that news be kept secret until publication by members and forbid members from furnishing AP news in advance to non-members or permitting other uses. This contractual/organizational requirement underpins AP's claim of protectable interest and is cited as the baseline obligation whose breach constitutes improper diversion of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfair/corrupt methods constituting unlawful appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtaining AP news 'unlawfully, and in some cases corruptly' by methods including (a) arranging with telegraph editors and other employees of member newspapers to communicate news to defendant for consideration before publication; (b) improper use of memberships to permit defendant representatives to copy news on receipt and sell/transmit it prior to publication; (c) copying news from early bulletins and early editions of member newspapers and systematically selling/transmitting the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill enumerates these as concrete unlawful practices used by defendant; in evaluating alleged piracy, courts will consider inducement/bribery of employees, misuse of membership privileges, and systematic copying from early editions/bulletins as indicia of tortious appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited acts sought in injunction (specific restraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: The injunctive relief sought (parts (a)–(e)) would restrain defendant from (a) inducing/procuring telegraph editors or employees of AP members to communicate or permit appropriation of AP news; (b) purchasing, obtaining or receiving AP news (directly or indirectly) which was furnished to AP members; (c) copying, receiving, selling, transmitting, or using AP news from bulletins or editions of member newspapers; (d) inducing members to violate AP charter and by-laws; (e) competing or aiding clients in competing by unfair or corrupt methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated prohibitions serve as the operative checklist for the scope of equitable relief the complainant asks the court to impose. They illustrate the specific behaviors an injunction may forbid when unfair competition/piracy is proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-value criteria for a news service
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the news service depends on promptness of service, accuracy, impartiality, earlier transmission to members than competitors, confidentiality prior to members' publication, and economical distribution (cost-sharing among members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complaint and affidavits repeatedly frame AP's protectable interest in terms of these service attributes; courts evaluate whether alleged appropriation undermines these business-value elements (e.g., by depriving members of prompt exclusive use) in determining harm and need for injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protectable interest in collected news until 'general publication' (no abandonment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A news gatherer is entitled to protection against a rival's sale/use of news until the gatherer has effectively abandoned it to the public by general publication; partial publication in some member papers does not necessarily effect abandonment if the gatherer's service aims at substantially simultaneous publication to its customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Hand reasons by analogy to trade secrets and other intangible-property protection: courts protect the gatherer's intangible business interest until sufficient time for general publication has elapsed. Whether abandonment has occurred depends on the gatherer's distribution practice and the time needed for its ordinary customers to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable protection period / time-window for competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: A rival should be prevented from selling or disseminating a news service's collected information 'until the ordinary customers of the gatherer within the field in which it operates have had sufficient time to receive and publish the news' — the opinion suggests three or four hours (and cites stock-quotation cases treating one hour as appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court proposes a pragmatic, geographically-sensitive time window (e.g., a few hours) as the period during which competitors' use of the news may be enjoined, balancing the gatherer's commercial interests and the public's interest in dissemination. Precedents (stock/grain quotation cases) may guide the specific duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable/injunctive protection for intangible business interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity protect intangible elements of business (goodwill, trade names, trade secrets, and the intangible property in a news-gathering enterprise) when appropriation by a competitor would result in distinctive injury to the enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites authorities and reasoning (e.g., Board of Trade v. Christie Grain & Stock Co.) that intangible commercial property merits equitable relief; thus injury to a news service's aggregate estate from piracy can justify injunctions even where copyright does not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tortious-injury standard for appropriation of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation of news gathered at substantial expense, sold as the competitor's own, and causing the original gatherer to be deprived of the fruits of its labor constitutes a tortious invasion of rights and actionable damage to the gatherer's business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will assess whether the competitor's conduct has (or will) cause concrete commercial injury (loss of customers/revenue, impairment of service value). Systematic and repeated appropriation that enables a rival to underprice or outcompete the gatherer supports relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of precedents (stock/grain quotation and other analogous cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions protecting stock and grain quotation services (e.g., National Telegraph News Co. v. Western Union) and cases protecting scenarios/plays/lectures/pictures after publication are analogous and support temporary protection for information carriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing news-piracy claims courts look to these analogies: (a) quotation agencies' right to prevent sale of received information for a limited time; (b) protection of intangible productions until dedication to the public. These precedents inform both the existence of a protectable right and practical remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance with public policy and dissemination interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection must be balanced against the public's interest in dissemination of news: while gatherers can withhold news prior to publication, the public benefit of prompt spread of information limits the duration and scope of exclusive protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court explicitly weighs public interest and frames protection as temporal and limited: preventing immediate misappropriation that frustrates the gatherer's service is permissible, but long-term suppression of dissemination would contradict public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence threshold and novelty in granting preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction should not be granted when the legal question is one of first impression and the matter is not 'sufficiently free from doubt' — equitable relief at the preliminary stage requires adequate certainty; novel or doubtful issues may counsel against immediate injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Hand denied a preliminary injunction on part of the claim for that reason while granting relief as to abstraction before publication where evidence of systematic infringement was strong. This criterion guides courts assessing requests for immediate relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic and culpable conduct by responsible representatives as justification for injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if some questionable practices were common business practice, proof of serious, systematic infraction by representatives in responsible positions (e.g., payments to telegraph editors, organized tapping of early editions) supports issuing an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will consider the pattern, scale, and responsibility level of wrongful acts; isolated or ambiguous conduct may not suffice, but documented systematic operations to divert news justify equitable restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of copyright: separate equitable/fiduciary remedies may apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if copyright law does not protect the raw news (or prior copyright cases are cited against such claims), equitable doctrines addressing unfair competition, trade secrets, and protection of intangible business interests can provide remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion distinguishes copyright limitations from equitable relief and instructs that lack of copyright protection does not preclude relief for unfair appropriation under equitable principles.
